html:
The Turkish alphabet is the Latin-based alphabet of 29 letters that replaced Arabic script for writing Turkish by a law of 1 November 1928.

For about a thousand years Turkish had been written in Arabic script, which fits Turkish vowels badly. Ottoman reformers had debated changes since the Tanzimat. Mustafa Kemal pushed through a full switch in a few months. He toured the country with a blackboard, teaching the letters himself.

New letters such as Ç, Ş, Ğ, Ö, Ü and the dotless I were added, so that each sound has one sign. After the law, newspapers, books and signs had to use the new script, and "nation's schools" taught adults to read.

The reform helped raise literacy, which had been low. It also cut young Turks off from Ottoman writing, all of which was now unreadable without study. Language reformers then purged many Arabic and Persian words. It sat alongside the Civil Code and end of the caliphate as a break with the Ottoman past.
sum: The Turkish alphabet is the Latin-based alphabet of 29 letters that replaced Arabic script for writing Turkish by a law of 1 November 1928.
